title: Planning the capstone
intro: A good capstone starts with a clear plan, not with a blank IDE window. In this lesson, you will turn the customer portal idea into a realistic MVP with user stories, a small data model, an API plan, milestones, and a definition of done.
body:
## From idea to buildable project

A capstone is different from a small exercise. You are no longer solving one isolated programming problem. You are building a small product from beginning to end, which means you need to decide **what to build, what not to build, and in what order to build it**.

Our capstone is a customer portal for a fictional company. Customers should be able to log in, see their orders and invoices, open support tickets, and chat about those tickets. Administrators should be able to manage support tickets.

That sounds simple, but it can quickly become a large project. Authentication, authorization, database relationships, REST APIs, frontend routing, forms, validation, chat, error handling, deployment, testing, and monitoring can all become separate workstreams.

The purpose of planning is not to predict every detail perfectly. The purpose is to create a **small enough first version that you can actually finish it**.

## Start with user stories

A user story describes a feature from the perspective of the person who needs it. A useful basic format is:

~~~diagram
{"type": "steps", "title": "From idea to issues", "steps": [{"label": "Idea", "sub": "a customer portal"}, {"label": "User stories", "sub": "As a customer, I want …"}, {"label": "Acceptance criteria", "sub": "Given / When / Then"}, {"label": "MoSCoW", "sub": "must · should · could · won't"}, {"label": "MVP backlog", "sub": "musts as GitHub issues"}]}
~~~

~~~text
As a <role>, I want <goal> so that <benefit>.
~~~

For example:

~~~text
As a customer, I want to see my orders so that I can check what I have purchased.
~~~

This format forces you to think about three things:

- **Role:** who needs the capability?
- **Goal:** what does that person want to do?
- **Benefit:** why does it matter?

Avoid writing stories as implementation tasks. “Create an OrderController” is a development task, not a user story. “As a customer, I want to view my orders so that I can track my purchases” describes the outcome instead.

A single story should ideally describe a meaningful slice of functionality. You can later break a large story into smaller stories if implementing it would require too much work for one sprint.

## Acceptance criteria make stories testable

A user story explains the desired outcome, but it is usually not precise enough for implementation by itself. **Acceptance criteria define what must be true for the story to be considered complete.**

For example:

~~~text
Story:
As a customer, I want to see my orders so that I can check my purchase history.

Acceptance criteria:
- The customer must be logged in.
- Only the customer's own orders are displayed.
- Orders are sorted by newest first.
- Each order shows its number, date, status, and total.
- An empty order history shows a useful empty state.
~~~

Acceptance criteria are useful for development, testing, and review. They also prevent a common problem: implementing something that technically works but does not actually satisfy the original requirement.

For the capstone, keep acceptance criteria short and observable. A reviewer should be able to look at the application and determine whether the criteria are satisfied.

## MoSCoW prioritization

Once you have a list of stories, you need to prioritize them. A useful technique is **MoSCoW prioritization**.

The four categories are:

- **Must:** essential for the product to work as an MVP.
- **Should:** important, but the first version can technically work without it.
- **Could:** useful improvements that can wait.
- **Won't:** explicitly excluded from the current scope.

For our customer portal, authentication is probably a Must. Customers need a way to securely access their data. Viewing orders and invoices are also likely Must features.

A real-time chat system might initially be a Should if a simpler ticket conversation can satisfy the requirement. Advanced notifications, file attachments, typing indicators, or a sophisticated search system could be Could items.

A mobile application could be a Won't for the capstone. That does not mean it is a bad idea. It means **you are deliberately protecting the project from scope creep**.

## Define the MVP

MVP means **Minimum Viable Product**. It is the smallest version of a product that delivers its core value.

For this capstone, a reasonable MVP could include:

1. Customer and admin authentication.
2. Customer access to their own orders.
3. Customer access to their own invoices.
4. Customers can create support tickets.
5. Customers can view and reply to ticket messages.
6. Admins can view and manage tickets.
7. Basic authorization so customers cannot access another customer's data.
8. A usable React interface and a deployed Spring Boot backend with a PostgreSQL database.

The MVP does not need every feature you could imagine. For example, you might postpone email notifications, file uploads, advanced analytics, full-text search, mobile apps, and real-time typing indicators.

A good rule is: **if removing a feature does not prevent the core user journey from working, consider moving it out of the MVP.**

## Sketch the data model

Before writing entities, create a simple conceptual model. Our core objects are User, Order, Invoice, Ticket, and Message.

~~~diagram
{"type": "flow", "title": "Customer portal data model", "nodes": [{"id": "u", "label": "User", "sub": "role: CUSTOMER · ADMIN", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "o", "label": "Order", "sub": "status · total", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "inv", "label": "Invoice", "sub": "number · pdfUrl", "kind": "db"}, {"id": "t", "label": "Ticket", "sub": "title · status", "kind": "db", "highlight": true}, {"id": "msg", "label": "Message", "sub": "body · createdAt", "kind": "db"}], "edges": [{"from": "u", "to": "o", "label": "1 : N"}, {"from": "o", "to": "inv", "label": "1 : 1"}, {"from": "u", "to": "t", "label": "1 : N"}, {"from": "t", "to": "msg", "label": "1 : N"}]}
~~~

A simplified relationship sketch could look like this:

~~~text
User
 ├── has many Orders
 ├── has many Invoices
 └── has many Tickets
          └── has many Messages

Order
 └── may have an Invoice

Ticket
 └── belongs to a customer
 └── contains Messages
~~~

This is deliberately not a complete database schema. At this stage, you are identifying the important concepts and relationships.

For example, a User could have an id, name, email, password hash, and role. An Order could contain an id, order number, customer reference, date, status, and total. A Ticket could contain an id, customer reference, subject, status, and timestamps. A Message could contain an id, ticket reference, author reference, text, and creation timestamp.

Do not start by creating every possible field. Start with the fields required to support the user stories.

## Design the REST API before coding controllers

A small API table makes backend development much easier because it turns vague requirements into concrete endpoints.

| Method | Endpoint | Purpose | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| POST | /api/auth/login | Log in | Public |
| GET | /api/orders | List current customer's orders | Customer |
| GET | /api/invoices | List current customer's invoices | Customer |
| GET | /api/tickets | List current customer's tickets | Customer |
| POST | /api/tickets | Open a ticket | Customer |
| GET | /api/tickets/{id}/messages | View ticket conversation | Customer/Admin |
| POST | /api/tickets/{id}/messages | Add a message | Customer/Admin |
| GET | /api/admin/tickets | List tickets | Admin |
| PATCH | /api/admin/tickets/{id} | Change ticket status | Admin |

The exact API can evolve as you build the application. The important thing is to decide the main resources and access rules early.

Notice the authorization distinction. A customer should not simply be allowed to request any order by putting another ID into the URL. The backend must verify that the authenticated customer owns the requested resource. This is a server-side security rule, not just a frontend visibility rule.

## Wireframes before polished UI

A wireframe is a rough visual plan of a screen. It does not need colors, animations, or final typography.

For the customer portal, sketch at least these screens:

- Login.
- Customer dashboard.
- Orders.
- Invoice list and invoice details.
- Ticket list.
- Ticket detail with conversation.
- New ticket form.

For administrators, sketch:

- Admin dashboard.
- Ticket queue.
- Ticket detail and conversation.

You can draw these on paper or use a simple wireframing tool. The goal is to answer questions before coding: What does the user see first? Where does navigation happen? Which information is visible? What happens when there is no data?

A rough wireframe can expose missing requirements surprisingly early.

## Organize the repository

A simple monorepo layout is a practical choice for this capstone:

~~~text
customer-portal/
├── frontend/
├── backend/
├── compose.yaml
├── README.md
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
~~~

The React application lives in `frontend`. The Spring Boot application lives in `backend`. Docker Compose can define the local PostgreSQL database and, later, the complete development stack.

The README should explain how to start the project, how configuration works, how to run tests, and where the major architectural decisions are documented.

Keep the structure boring. The capstone is supposed to demonstrate engineering skills, not your ability to invent a complicated repository layout.

## Plan milestones instead of one giant deadline

Break the project into milestones with a clear outcome.

A possible plan is:

**Milestone 1 — Foundation**

Create the repositories, Spring Boot application, React application, PostgreSQL setup, Docker Compose configuration, basic CI, and initial project documentation.

**Milestone 2 — Authentication and authorization**

Implement login, JWT-based authentication, roles, protected frontend routes, and backend authorization.

**Milestone 3 — Customer data**

Implement users, orders, invoices, database migrations, repositories, services, REST endpoints, and customer-facing screens.

**Milestone 4 — Support tickets**

Add ticket creation, ticket lists, ticket details, messages, and authorization rules.

**Milestone 5 — Admin workflow**

Build the admin ticket queue, ticket management, and role-protected screens.

**Milestone 6 — Quality and deployment**

Add automated tests, error handling, logging, monitoring basics, production configuration, and deployment.

The milestone names are less important than the rule behind them: **each milestone should produce something demonstrably usable.**

## Use GitHub Projects as your control panel

A GitHub Projects board can turn your plan into visible work. A simple board could contain:

~~~text
Backlog → Ready → In Progress → Review → Done
~~~

Create an issue for each user story or meaningful technical task. Link related pull requests to the issues. Add priority, milestone, and estimated effort where useful.

Avoid creating hundreds of tiny issues. “Implement customer orders” can be a useful story, while “create variable called orders” is not.

The board should answer three questions quickly:

1. What needs to be done?
2. What am I working on now?
3. What is blocking progress?

This is particularly useful for a solo capstone because you are acting as developer, product owner, tester, and project manager at the same time.

## Time boxing and sprint capacity

A time box is a fixed amount of time available for a piece of work. Instead of asking, “How long will everything take?”, decide how much capacity you have and select work that fits.

~~~callout tip Plan for 70% of your time
If you can spend 10 hours a week, plan 7 hours of stories. The rest goes to bugs, setup surprises and learning — and that is normal, not failure.
~~~

You can estimate stories with simple points such as 1, 2, 3, 5, and 8. The numbers are relative rather than exact hours.

Suppose your sprint capacity is 8 points:

~~~text
MUST:   Login        3
MUST:   Orders       5
SHOULD: Tickets      5
COULD:  Dashboard    2
~~~

The first two Must stories consume all 8 points. The ticket feature waits for the next sprint.

The exercise in this lesson implements a small sprint planner. It prioritizes Must, Should, and Could stories, then chooses stories that still fit the remaining capacity. Importantly, it skips an oversized story and continues checking smaller stories later in the list. This is a useful reminder that capacity planning is not simply “take the first N items.”

If the Must stories themselves cannot fit into the available capacity, the plan is invalid. You need to increase capacity, reduce scope, or split the stories.

## Definition of Done

A Definition of Done is a shared checklist describing what “complete” means. Without one, “finished” often means “the code works on my machine.”

For this capstone, a story might be Done when:

- The acceptance criteria are satisfied.
- Backend validation is implemented.
- Authorization is enforced server-side.
- Automated tests cover important behavior.
- The frontend handles loading, success, and error states.
- The code is reviewed or self-reviewed.
- The feature works with the project's normal local setup.
- Relevant documentation is updated.
- CI passes.

Not every tiny task needs every item individually, but your final capstone should meet a consistent quality standard.

## Identify risks early

A risk is something that could prevent the project from succeeding. Write down risks before they become emergencies.

Typical risks for this capstone include:

- **Scope risk:** too many features are added after development starts.
- **Authentication risk:** security work takes longer than expected.
- **Data-model risk:** relationships are changed repeatedly because they were not thought through.
- **Integration risk:** frontend and backend assumptions do not match.
- **Deployment risk:** production configuration is left until the final day.
- **Time risk:** the project is too ambitious for the available hours.

For each major risk, define a mitigation. For example, deployment risk can be reduced by deploying a minimal version early rather than waiting until every feature is finished.

## Common mistakes

### Starting with implementation instead of scope

Opening IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition and immediately creating entities can feel productive, but you may be implementing the wrong thing. Start with stories, priorities, and the MVP.

### Making every feature a Must

If everything is a Must, nothing is actually prioritized. A useful MVP requires saying no to some good ideas.

### Writing vague stories

“As a customer, I want a better experience” is not specific enough to implement or test. Define a concrete goal and a concrete benefit.

### Treating the frontend as the security boundary

Hiding an admin button is not authorization. The backend must enforce access to protected resources.

### Waiting until the end to deploy

A project that only works locally is not finished. Get a minimal deployment working early enough that infrastructure problems have time to surface.

### Estimating every task perfectly

Planning is useful even when estimates are wrong. Use time boxes and review your progress regularly rather than pretending that a six-week plan can predict every hour.

## Your capstone planning checklist

Before writing substantial application code, you should be able to answer:

- Who are the main users?
- What are the Must-have stories?
- What is explicitly outside the MVP?
- What are the core entities and relationships?
- What are the main API endpoints?
- What screens does each user need?
- What is the repository structure?
- What are the milestones?
- Where is the work tracked?
- What is the current sprint capacity?
- What risks could derail the project?
- What does Done mean?

You do not need a perfect plan. You need a **small, visible, adjustable plan that makes the next piece of work obvious**.

The next lessons can then focus on building the system rather than continuously deciding what the system is supposed to be.
takeaways: User stories describe value from the user's perspective.
Acceptance criteria make requirements observable and testable.
MoSCoW helps protect the MVP from scope creep.
A small data model and REST API plan reduce implementation uncertainty.
Milestones, time boxes, and GitHub Projects turn the plan into actionable work.
A Definition of Done and risk list make completion and project health explicit.

quiz.question: Which is the best example of a user story?
options: Create an OrderController in Spring Boot.
As a customer, I want to see my orders so that I can check my purchase history.
Add a GET endpoint for orders.
Create the orders table in PostgreSQL.
quiz.explanation: A user story describes a user's role, goal, and benefit. The other options are implementation tasks.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of acceptance criteria?
options: To define when a story can be considered complete.
To choose the programming language.
To replace automated tests entirely.
To describe the database indexes.
quiz.explanation: Acceptance criteria describe observable conditions that must be satisfied for the story to be accepted.

quiz.question: Which MoSCoW category contains functionality that is explicitly excluded from the current scope?
options: Must
Should
Could
Won't
quiz.explanation: Won't represents functionality that is deliberately outside the current scope or release.

quiz.question: Why should authorization be enforced by the backend?
options: Because frontend components cannot contain buttons.
Because the backend is the only place where databases can be used.
Because a user can bypass frontend restrictions and call the API directly.
Because React cannot display protected data.
quiz.explanation: Frontend restrictions improve the user experience, but they are not a security boundary. The backend must verify permissions for protected operations.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a time box?
options: To guarantee that every estimate is exactly correct.
To define a fixed amount of available time and limit the work selected for it.
To eliminate the need for priorities.
To make every feature a Must-have.
quiz.explanation: A time box gives you a fixed capacity and helps you select work that can realistically fit within that capacity.

exercise.title: Build a sprint planner and story validator
exercise.task:
Write exactly two functions: `planSprint(stories, capacity)` and `validateStory(text)`.

`planSprint(stories, capacity)` receives an array of stories shaped like `{ id, title, priority, points }`, where priority is `must`, `should`, `could`, or `wont`. Ignore `wont` stories. Sort the remaining stories by priority in this exact order: `must`, `should`, `could`; then by `points` ascending; then by `id` using normal string comparison. Walk through the sorted list and select each story whose points still fit in the remaining capacity. If a story does not fit, skip it and continue with the next story. Return `{ selected: [ids in selection order], used: total points, leftover: [ids not selected, excluding wont, in sorted order] }`. If the total points of the Must stories alone exceed the capacity, throw an Error whose message contains `must`. Do not mutate the input array or its story objects.

`validateStory(text)` validates the user-story format `As a <role>, I want <goal> so that <benefit>` case-insensitively. The beginning may use either `As a` or `As an`. The text must contain the separators `, I want ` and ` so that `, and the role, goal, and benefit must all be non-empty after trimming. Return `{ valid: boolean, role, goal, benefit }`. For an invalid story, return `valid: false` and empty strings for all three parts.
exercise.hint: For `planSprint`, separate the problem into three steps: filter and sort the eligible stories, calculate the total Must points before selecting anything, then walk through the sorted list while tracking used capacity. For `validateStory`, a single case-insensitive regular expression can capture the role, goal, and benefit, but remember that both `a` and `an` are valid articles and that every captured part must be non-empty after trimming.

tests.name: It prioritizes must, should, and could stories in that order
It sorts equal-priority stories by points and then by id
It skips a story that does not fit and continues with later stories
It ignores wont stories
It throws when must stories alone exceed capacity
It reports leftover eligible stories in sorted order
It does not mutate the input stories
It validates a standard customer story
It accepts As an and is case insensitive
It rejects missing role, goal, or benefit
It rejects non-string input safely
